# Isaiah 18: verse-by-verse research notes

**Before you use these notes:** I ran out of searches before I could check several sources. I found nothing from the Wesley Center, the Lutheran sites, the Pentecostal sites, the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or the Catholic and Orthodox sites. So those views are left out. Where I name a teacher's tradition (for example "Reformed"), that label is mine, not the page's.

---

## Overview

- Guzik (Enduring Word) reads the chapter this way: Cush (Ethiopia) offers Judah an alliance against Assyria. God's main message is straightforward: Judah doesn't need Ethiopian help because the LORD is fully capable of handling Assyria on His own. He also quotes older writers who call it the hardest chapter in Isaiah. Bultema calls it "the most difficult one of all the sixty-six chapters of Isaiah". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- Bible Hub's overview gives the background. Around 715-701 BC, the Nubian (25th) dynasty ruled Egypt from Cush. Envoys from Cush urged Judah to join a coalition against Assyria. The chapter fits Isaiah's larger counsel: trust the LORD, not foreign alliances (see Isaiah 30–31). https://biblehub.com/isaiah/18.htm
- Ellicott says King Tirhakah's moves had raised the hopes of Hezekiah's advisers as put their trust in an arm of flesh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-1.htm

---

## v. 1: "Woe to the land of whirring wings"

**Traditional readings**
- **What "whirring wings" means**
  - Guzik: The Nile Valley is famous for its many whirring insects. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
  - Ellicott lists three options: an imperial eagle, the winged disk that was a symbol of Ethiopian rule, or swarms of tsetse flies (Ellicott's word is "tse-tse fly") . He prefers the winged disk and supports it with an Egyptian inscription in which chiefs ask to be "under thy shadow." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
  - Barnes thinks the meaning is, perhaps, not possible to determine... its meaning must be left to conjecture. He slightly prefers the ancient Greek and Aramaic reading of ships with sails spread like wings . https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-1.html
  - Utley (bible.org) lists many possible meanings of the Hebrew root: buzzing insects, a whizzing spear, locusts, a percussion instrument, or shadow. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18
- **Where Cush is**
  - Grogan, quoted by Guzik, says the term covers a much larger area than present-day Ethiopia – an area including the Sudan and Somalia. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
  - Ellicott places "beyond the rivers" in the region of the White and Blue Nile . https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-1.htm

**Where interpreters differ: is "woe" a threat or a greeting?**
- **A threat of judgment**
  - Poole says God, in defending His church, will destroy this nation . https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/18.htm
  - Matthew Henry: here is a woe denounced against it, for God has, upon his people's account, a quarrel with it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_018.cfm
- **A call for attention ("Ho!")**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) say the Hebrew does not express a threat, but is an appeal calling attention. Isaiah speaks *to* the Ethiopians, not *against* them . https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_018.cfm
  - Benson follows Bishop Lowth's rendering, "Ho!" . https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-1.htm
- **Either is possible**
  - Barnes says it may be a greeting or a word of judgment . https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-1.htm
  - Utley notes the word usually announces judgment, but here it may express sympathy. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18

**Historical Reformed and Methodist voices**
- Calvin reads the "wings" as a sign of a well-harboured, wealthy sea trade . https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-1.html
- Clarke (Methodist) says the wings may be the sails of many ships . https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-1.html

---

## v. 2: Papyrus boats and the "tall and smooth-skinned" people

**Traditional readings**
- **The envoys**
  - Guzik pictures Ethiopian ambassadors arriving to form an alliance against Assyria . https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
  - Ellicott says the envoys came down the Nile in papyrus boats to Hezekiah. The words "Go, swift messengers" are Isaiah himself sending them home. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- **The papyrus boats**
  - Barnes links the Hebrew word to the "ark of bulrushes" that carried baby Moses (Exodus 2:3). He says it seems to fix the scene of this prophecy to the region of the Nile. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
  - Utley notes that such boats were also used on the Tigris and Euphrates. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18
- **"A powerful nation"**
  - Barnes takes the old phrase "meted out" to mean a nation that stretched measuring lines over *others*, that is, conquered them . https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
  - Utley says several Hebrew phrases here are uncertain. One Jewish translation renders "powerful" as a description of their strange-sounding language. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18

**Where interpreters differ: who is being described?**
- **Ethiopia**
  - Ellicott reads "tall and polished" instead of the King James "scattered and peeled." He says that some, "with less probability," apply the words to Israel instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- **God's own people**
  - Matthew Henry applies it to them: they are trampled, yet cast down, but not deserted, not destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
- **Who is told to "go"?**
  - Utley lists possible senders: Cush, Egypt, mercenaries south of Cush, Assyria, or all human armies opposed to God. He adds that Isaiah often shifts between his own day and the end of history. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18
- **Calvin's reading (Reformed)**
  - Calvin takes the command as given in God's name. If so, God delays his aid till they are brought to a state of despair. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html

---

## v. 3: The banner and the trumpet

- Ellicott says the clauses are general ("when a banner is raised"). All nations, Ethiopia included, are to watch for the signal of Assyria's downfall. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the world's attention is drawn to the destruction of Asshur by Jehovah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-1.htm
- Guzik: If God had wanted to muster an army against Assyria, He would have raised a banner or sounded a trumpet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- Matthew Henry turns it into an appeal: Let all enlist under God's banner. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
- Utley lists seven possible senders and audiences for the verse. He says the signals could mean judgment (vv. 5–6) or salvation (v. 7). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18

---

## v. 4: God "quietly looks on"

**Traditional readings**
- Guzik: God turned down the alliance because He could deal with Assyria Himself . He also notes that there is no rebuke or judgment against Ethiopia announced in this chapter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- Ellicott says the images show God's calm, deliberate judgment. God is "unhasting and unresting," watching from His throne as the fruit ripens. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- Matthew Henry says God's "rest" does not mean He is tired. It means He is perfectly at peace amid all the world's upheavals , and his eye and his heart are... upon it for good continually. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
- Utley says God's "dwelling place" may be the temple or heaven. He contrasts heaven's calm with earth's chaos, much as Revelation does . https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18
- Bible Hub's overview draws the lesson that God's timing often involves a silent interval; faith waits (Isaiah 30:15). https://biblehub.com/isaiah/18.htm

**Where interpreters differ: what does God watch over?**
- Poole mentions "learned men" who take the verse as God watching over His church. He rejects this as altogether unsuitable to the scope and business of the chapter, which is about Egypt and Ethiopia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/18.htm
- Matthew Henry takes the church reading: Zion is his rest for ever, where he will dwell. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html

---

## v. 5: The pruning knife

- Guzik: God can "prune" Assyria all by Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- Ellicott: once the grape has ripened, God comes as Lord of the vineyard and cuts off the branches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- Utley calls it an agricultural picture of swift judgment (compare 17:14). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18
- Bible Hub's overview compares God to a farmer waiting for the right moment to harvest. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/18.htm

---

## v. 6: Left for birds and beasts

- Ellicott says the picture and the reality blend together. The cut-off "grapes" are the unburied bodies of the Assyrian army. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- Guzik agrees: the Assyrian army will be so completely destroyed that it is left for the birds of prey . https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- Chuck Smith says there are so many bodies that animals are still eating the remains through the winter . https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
- Matthew Henry draws a lesson from it: God's people are protected in every season, while their enemies are exposed in every season . https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-7.htm

---

## v. 7: Gifts brought to Mount Zion

**Traditional readings**
- Guzik: instead of Israelites carrying alliance news to Ethiopia, Ethiopians will come to worship at Zion . https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- Ellicott says the people themselves are the gift. He compares Psalm 68:31 ("Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God") and Psalm 87. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm
- Utley notes that the standard Hebrew text has no "from," so the people may be the offering. The Dead Sea Scrolls, the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and the Latin Vulgate do have "from." He says it may mean a remnant of Cush or the whole Gentile world, and that the enemies of vv. 1–2 become worshippers. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-18
- Matthew Henry says gifts must come to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts. In other words, worship must be offered in the way God has appointed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html

**Where interpreters differ: when is this fulfilled?**
- **Soon after the events.** Ellicott says envoys who fit Isaiah's words were probably found among the envoys mentioned in 2Chronicles 32:23. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/18-7.htm
- **Through the gospel.** Poole: He speaks of their conversion to God and Christ by the preaching of the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/18.htm
- **Both.** Guzik says it may have been partly fulfilled near Isaiah's time. It was fulfilled in the Ethiopian official of Acts 8:26–40, and in the strong Ethiopian church of the first few centuries, and the enduring Ethiopian church today. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-18/
- **A minority view.** Ellicott notes that some apply this verse, like v. 2, to Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/18.htm

---

## Debated popular modern teaching

- **America in Isaiah 18 (vv. 1, 2 and 7).** Chuck Smith reports that some see the United States here, pointing to the eagle with spread wings above the American flag. He rejects it: it is rather far-fetched. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/18-2.html
- I found no Catholic, Orthodox, prosperity, Word of Faith or hyper-grace material on this chapter.
